query: For single-phase ZrB2 ceramic, which requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and may lack the strength and structural integrity needed for service, what single intervention could lower the required preparation temperature and reduce the holes and eventual component failure caused by prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention and its mechanism, predict its performance compared with conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2, define the relevant preparation and service boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and describe a controlled preparation, integrity, and long-duration exposure experiment that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing conventional high‐temperature sintering with spark plasma sintering (SPS) for single‐phase ZrB2 ceramics will enable densification at lower temperatures (around 2000°C vs. >2300°C), thereby producing a microstructure with reduced residual porosity and enhanced strength that resists hole formation and component failure during prolonged liquid plating exposure.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase ZrB2 ceramic prepared by conventional pressureless sintering above 2300°C, typically featuring a less‐dense, porous microstructure that is prone to surface attack during long-term liquid plating.
generation.intervention: Utilize spark plasma sintering (SPS) with a rapid heating rate and short dwell time to consolidate ZrB2 powders at a reduced sintering temperature (approximately 2000°C).
generation.conditions: The SPS process is carried out in an inert (argon) atmosphere with a controlled temperature profile (rapid ramp to ~2000°C with minimal hold time) to achieve full densification. Subsequently, both SPS-processed and conventionally sintered samples are exposed to a simulated liquid plating bath (e.g., at 90°C in the relevant plating solution) for an extended duration (e.g., 100 hours) to assess resistance to pore/void formation and mechanical integrity.
generation.structural_mediator: A finer, more homogeneous microstructure with significantly reduced residual porosity and grain boundary defects.
generation.mechanism: SPS applies pulsed electric currents and uniaxial pressure that promote rapid densification at lower temperatures. This minimizes the time available for grain growth and pore coarsening, resulting in a denser ceramic that offers improved mechanical strength and a barrier against liquid penetration and ensuing defect propagation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with conventionally sintered ZrB2 ceramics, the SPS-processed ceramics are expected to achieve full densification at a lower preparation temperature, exhibit higher flexural and compressive strength, and show markedly reduced formation of holes or related failures during prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath.
generation.baseline: Conventional single-phase ZrB2 fabricated above 2300°C by pressureless sintering, which typically exhibits higher porosity and lower mechanical integrity when exposed to aggressive liquid plating conditions.
generation.boundary: Preparation boundary: conventional sintering above 2300°C versus SPS at ~2000°C; Service boundary: extended exposure (e.g., 100 hours) in a liquid plating bath environment (around 90°C) used in plating applications.
generation.uncertainty: The exact reduction in sintering temperature necessary to achieve equivalent or improved densification and the quantitative enhancement in resistance to liquid plating damage remain to be determined; optimal SPS parameters may require further fine-tuning.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of single-phase ZrB2 ceramic samples from identical starting powders. One set is consolidated by conventional pressureless sintering at >2300°C, and the other set is processed using SPS at ~2000°C with optimized parameters (rapid heating and short dwell time). All samples will then be characterized for density (e.g., via Archimedes’ method) and microstructure (using SEM). Subsequently, expose both sets to a controlled liquid plating bath (maintained at ~90°C) for 100 hours. After exposure, assess changes in surface integrity (via SEM imaging for hole/porosity development) and measure mechanical properties (e.g., flexural strength, fracture toughness).
measurements: Density and porosity via Archimedes method
Microstructural evaluation using SEM and possibly TEM for grain and pore analysis
Mechanical strength tests (flexural/compressive strength) before and after exposure
Quantitative assessment of surface damage (hole formation) after liquid plating exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SPS-processed ZrB2 samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in densification (lower porosity), mechanical strength, and resistance to hole formation compared to conventional samples following the liquid plating exposure, then the hypothesis that SPS processing at lower temperatures improves the ceramic's performance is falsified.

The results are presented in Figure 2. From the graph, it is evident that (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb)B2, (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta)B2, (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Mo)B2, and (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta, Mo)B2 all exhibit a single-phase structure, with their respective lattice parameters listed in Table 1. In contrast, (Ti, Zr, Hf, Ta, W)B2 and (Ti, Zr, Hf, Mo, W)B2 show variations. In the XRD patterns of (Ti, Zr, Hf, Ta, W)B2 and (Ti, Zr, Hf, Mo, W)B2 systems, in addition to the high-entropy phase, impurity phases such as (Mo, W)2B5, W2B5, and minor amounts of (Ti, Zr, Hf, Mo, W)C and B4C were observed. Notably, these non-single-phase (Ti, Zr, Hf, Ta, W)B2 and (Ti, Zr, Hf, Mo, W)B2 systems corresponded to higher δ values. Hence, it is less likely to form single-phase, high-entropy borides when δ exceeds 3.9%. In the upcoming experiments, our focus will be on (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta)B2, which boasts the smallest δ value.
